summary:
Could a giant planet still hide beyond Neptune? Planet X — also called Planet Nine — is a hypothesis from 2016: a planet of roughly 4–10 Earth masses, 300–800 AU from the Sun, proposed from the clustering of distant objects. It has not been found — or ruled out.

Our team, THE SCARERS, built a free web tool that lets anyone join the search with NASA's SPHEREx data. SPHEREx, launched in March 2025, is mapping the whole sky in near-infrared light (0.75–5.0 µm, 102 bands); its first data release (DR1) came out on 12 November 2026.

The tool lets you pick a sky region, blink between real photos taken decades apart to spot what moved, check candidates against known catalogs, and export your list as CSV or JSON. Every photo is a real NASA SkyView image — nothing is simulated. Our demo is Barnard's star, the fastest-moving star in the sky. We are honest about the limits: a cold Planet Nine would peak outside SPHEREx's range, so SPHEREx helps with repeated all-sky coverage, and a third epoch is needed to confirm anything. We do not claim a discovery — we built a tool so anyone can take part in the search.
details:
What it does and how it works

Our tool is a free public web page that lets anyone search for Planet X in SPHEREx data. Pick a sky region — or enter coordinates — and blink between real photos of the same sky taken decades apart: DSS plates from the 1950s and DSS2 from the 1980s–90s, served by NASA SkyView. Anything that moved between epochs stands out. The comparator offers blink, mix, difference and side-by-side modes, and the visible-change demo is Barnard's star, the fastest-moving star in the sky. An advanced searcher builds the real SIA2 query against the SPHEREx archive at IRSA (with a coordinate guide and an hours/minutes/seconds-to-degrees converter), an embedded Aladin Lite viewer follows the chosen region, and a candidate list lets you save, verify and export candidates as CSV or JSON.

Benefits and expected impact

Anyone — student, teacher, amateur astronomer — can join a real search for a hidden planet with nothing more than a browser. It turns a hard archival problem into something you can see with your own eyes, and it shows how astronomers actually find moving objects. If a candidate survives verification, it can be shared with the community for follow-up.

Tools and technologies

A single self-contained web page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript — no build step, no backend), hosted free on GitHub Pages. Data comes live from NASA SkyView, the IRSA SPHEREx archive (SIA2 queries and FITS cutouts), the CDS Aladin Lite viewer, the Gaia archive and the AWS S3 public mirror of SPHEREx files. The team worked in GitHub with collaborators, commits and Pages.

What makes it creative

Instead of asking users to download FITS files or run code, it brings the blink-comparator method — the same one Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto — to the browser, with real photos, and centers the experience on a star you can actually watch move.

What the team considered

Real data only, nothing simulated; honest limits (a cold Planet Nine peaks outside SPHEREx's range; two epochs do not fix an orbit; the IRSA server is intermittent and the page says so); access for non-experts (a simple region selector, a 20-second explainer, a 5-step guided demo and a glossary); and open source (MIT), so anyone can reuse it.
